message.content: Aluminum conducts heat faster than cast iron, so a thin aluminum pan warms up almost immediately. Conducting heat and storing it are separate properties: conduction is how quickly heat moves through a material, while heat capacity determines how much energy it holds for a given temperature rise. Cast iron is much denser. A thick 10-inch cast-iron skillet can weigh several times more than a thin aluminum pan of the same diameter, so it contains far more metal and has greater thermal mass. It takes more energy to heat, then releases that energy more slowly. Fully preheat a cast-iron skillet, then sear a steak. When the cool meat hits the surface, the heavy pan can keep the surface sizzling through the first minute or so and help build a brown crust. A thin aluminum pan may cool sharply at the contact point even though heat moves through it fast. One limitation: this assumes similar pan size and thickness. A thick aluminum pan or one with a heavy base can also store enough heat to sear a steak, and a very thin cast-iron pan would not stay hot as long.
